ricinus Ticks and Rodents from Slovakia
Zuzana Hamšíková1 & Claudia Coipan2 & Lenka Mahríková1 & Lenka Minichová3 &

Abstract Borrelia miyamotoi causes relapsing fever in
humans. The occurrence of this spirochete has been reported
in Ixodes ricinus and wildlife, but there are still gaps in the
knowledge of its eco-epidemiology and public health impact.

skin biopsies from rodents captured in Slovakia were screened
for the presence of
B
. miyamotoi and Borrelia burgdorferi s.l.

Introduction
Borrelia miyamotoi is a tick-borne relapsing fever spirochete. It
is transmitted by species of the Ixodes genus in temperate re-
gions of the northern hemisphere and is considered an emerging
pathogen [1–5]. B. miyamotoi was first detected in Ixodes
persulcatus in Japan [6], and since then, it has been found in
Ixodes spp. in the USA [7, 8] and Canada [9] and I. persulcatus
in Russia [10, 11] and Estonia [12]. B. miyamotoi-infected
questing and engorged Ixodes ricinus ticks have been found
in different European countries and habitat types, including
urban and suburban parks [8, 13–25]. Transovarial transmission
of B. miyamotoi from tick females to their progeny exists and
contributes to the maintenance of the infection in natural foci
[26–28]. Wild-living rodents have been indicated as reservoir
hosts of B. miyamotoi in North America [7, 29], Japan [30], and
Europe [19, 23, 31]. The role of other vertebrates such as free-
living ruminants or ground-dwelling and passerine birds as res-
ervoirs or carriers of infected ticks is suggested [4, 32].
B. miyamotoi has been recognized as a human pathogen
only recently, with relapsing fever cases reported, e.g. in
Russia [33], North America [34], the Netherlands [35],
Japan [36], and Germany [37]. On the other hand, Lyme
borreliosis caused by spirochetes of the Borrelia burgdorferi

sensu lato (s.l.) complex is the most common tick-borne hu-
man infection in the northern hemisphere [38, 39]. B.
burgdorferi s.l. and B. miyamotoi probably share the same
vector ticks [16, 20, 28] and rodent hosts [4, 31], whereby
Borrelia afzelii and Borrelia bavariensis have been found
specifically associated to European rodents [40–42].
In Slovakia, B. miyamotoi was detected first in questing I.
ricinus from a suburban forest close to Bratislava town [43]
and subsequently in a mountainous region in the central part
of the country [24], indicating that endemic foci exist in
Slovakia. No clinical cases of tick-borne relapsing fever have
been reported from Slovakia [44]. The findings of
B
miyamotoi in questing ticks suggest, however, that humans
may be at risk of infection.
Because B. miyamotoi and spirochetes of the B. burgdorferi
s.l. complex share vectors, they were found to co-occur in nat-
ural foci and mixed infections have also been reported in ticks
[9, 12, 19]. This indicates a possible risk of co-infections of
humans with both pathogens and should be considered in diag-
nosis of the disease [4, 21].
The aims of this study were (1) to determine the prevalence
of B. miyamotoi in questing I. ricinus ticks and rodents from
urban/suburban and natural sites in southwestern Slovakia, (2)
to molecularly characterize the B. miyamotoi isolates, (3) to
assess the role of rodents in the natural circulation of
B
miyamotoi, and (4) to determine the rate of co-infection of
B. miyamotoi and B. burgdorferi s.l. genospecies in ticks
and rodents.
Material and Methods
Ticks and Rodents
Questing ticks and rodent tissues were available from a previ-
ous study conducted in southwestern Slovakia during 2011–
2014 [45]. From the tick collections from urban/suburban lo-
cations in Bratislava and from a non-fragmented deciduous
forest at Fúgelka, 1696 questing I. ricinus (547 nymphs,
1149 adults) were randomly selected: Bratislava—282
nymphs, 574 adults; Fúgelka—265 nymphs, 575 adults.
Skin samples (ear biopsies) were gathered from 605 rodents:
300 from Bratislava; 305 from Fúgelka. Genomic DNA from
ticks and rodent skin was extracted with the Macherey Nagel
Nucleospin Tissue kit [45]. DNA lysates derived from indi-
vidual ticks
5 ~ \mu \mathrm { l }
each) were pooled. In total, 340 pooled
samples (pool size 3–7) were examined for B. burgdorferi
s.l. and B. miyamotoi by real-time polymerase chain reaction
(qPCR). Individual ticks from pools which tested positive for
B. miyamotoi were further examined for the presence of
B
miyamotoi and B. burgdorferi s.l. genospecies by convention-
al PCR and sequencing. All rodent skin samples were
analysed individually.
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
For the detection of B. burgdorferi s.l. and B. miyamotoi, a
triplex qPCR, targeting ospA and flaB genes, was performed
with primers previously described [35, 46]. The sequences of
primers and probes, as well as the qPCR settings are given in
the Online Resource 1 (Table S1). For each run, positive and
negative controls and blank samples were included. Samples
were considered positive with Ct values below 38 cycles.
The qPCR-positive samples were examined by conven-
tional PCR targeting the glycerophosphodiester phosphodies-
terase gene
( g l p Q )
of B. miyamotoi and the 5S-23S rDNA
intergenic spacer (IGS) of B. burgdorferi s.l., according to
the protocols described elsewhere [35, 47].
PCR products were purified by using ExoSAP-IT
\textsuperscript { \textregistered }
PCR
Product Cleanup (Affymetrix USB), and amplicons were se-
quenced on an ABI3730XL sequencer from Life
Technologies™.
Sequence Analysis
Sequences were assembled, edited, and aligned with
BioNumerics v. 7.6.1 software. Representative sequences
were submitted to the GenBank (see Tables S2, S3). The
relatedness among the B. miyamotoi glpQ sequences as well
as among the B. burgdorferi s.l. IGS sequences was assessed
by phylogenetic analysis. A 689 nt fragment of glpQ
trimmed to nucleotides 656747 to 657435 of
B
. miyamotoi
FR64b complete genome (GenBank No. CP004217) was
used for phylogenetic analysis of B. miyamotoi. For the
phylogeny of B. burgdorferi s.l., an IGS fragment trimmed
to nucleotides between positions 438838 and 439196 of
whole genome sequence of B. afzelii strain PKo (GenBank
No. CP002933) was used. Maximum likelihood (ML) phy-
logenetic trees were built with MEGA 7.0.14, using the
General Time Reversible model and 100 bootstrap repli-
cates. For comparative purposes, glpQ sequences of
B
miyamotoi, available in GenBank, from worldwide sources
and regions were used. The tree for B. miyamotoi was rooted
with Borrelia lonestari while that for B. burgdorferi s.l. with
Borrelia turdi.
Statistical Analyses
Fisher’s exact test or the chi-square test were used to test for
associations between B. miyamotoi infection rates in ticks and
their developmental stage or site, as well as for associations
between B. miyamotoi and B. burgdorferi s.l. infection rates in
rodents and rodent species or site. A

were not included in the analyses of species. In I. ricinus,
B
burgdorferi s.l. infection rates were analysed for pooled sam-
ples (pool size 3–7) by the maximum likelihood estimation

Phylogenetic Analysis
Analysis of the glpQ sequences confirmed the presence of
B
miyamotoi in ticks and rodent skin. The list of representative
sequences with GenBank accession numbers and their source
(tick, rodent, site) from this study are given in Table S2. All
analysed DNA sequences were
identical compared to
each other and showed high identity with sequences of the
B
miyamotoi from I. ricinus in the Netherlands (AB824855),
from the cerebrospinal fluid of a human patient in the
Netherlands (AB824730), from a questing I. ricinus nymph
in Hungary (LC006118), and an engorged I. ricinus larva from
A. flavicollis in Hungary (LC006120) (Fig. 1). The genetic
difference from the Asian and American B. miyamotoi was
and
, respectively.
Analysis of IGS sequences indicated the presence of four
B. burgdorferi s.l. genospecies in questing ticks and three
genospecies in rodents. The majority were represented by
B
afzelii (Fig. 2). B. garinii and B. bavariensis were found not
only in questing ticks, but also in A. flavicollis, whereas
B
valaisiana was identified only in ticks. The list of selected
sequences with GenBank accession numbers and their source
(tick, rodent, site) from this study are given in Table S3.
Discussion
In the current study, DNA of relapsing fever (B. miyamotoi)
and Lyme disease (B. burgdorferi s.l.) spirochetes was simul-
taneously detected in questing I. ricinus ticks and rodents
captured in southwestern Slovakia. Overall prevalence of in-
fection was lower for
B
. miyamotoi than B. burgdorferi s.l. in
ticks (1.7 vs.
) as well as rodents (7.1 vs.
). The
Borrelia prevalences in questing I. ricinus are in the range
reported from other locations in Europe including Slovakia:
B. miyamotoi
[5, 24, 49]; B. burgdorferi s.l.
[24, 50–52]. According to Barbour et al. [7] or Wagemakers
et al. [4], the relatively low prevalence of B. miyamotoi in
questing Ixodes spp. could be either due to an adverse effect
of the spirochete on survival of infected ticks, or a result of a
low acquisition rate from infected hosts by ticks due to a lower
load of B. miyamotoi in infected skin in comparison with
B
burgdorferi s.l.
In general, spatial, temporal, and interstadial variations in
prevalence and genetic diversity of tick-borne microorganisms,
including Borrelia, are phenomena described for a number of
sites across Europe [16, 22, 47, 50, 51, 53]. We assume that the
observed prevalences of the relapsing fever and Lyme disease
spirochetes in different developmental stages of questing I.
ricinus ticks and the genetic variability of B. burgdorferi s.l.
are determined by the tick phenology and physiology, local hab-
itat structure, and vertebrate host spectrum. Consistent with re-
sults of other studies [17, 19, 21–23, 54, 55], we found a signif-
icantly higher proportion of questing I. ricinus ticks infected with
B. burgdorferi s.l. compared to B. miyamotoi. B. afzelii was the
prevailing genospecies, followed by B. garinii, B. valaisiana,
and B. bavariensis. Our results on the predominance of the
rodent-associated B. afzelii are in line with reports from a number
of locations in Europe [17, 47, 53, 54] and support the impor-
tance of rodents in the transmission cycles of Borrelia species
vectored by I. ricinus [4, 23, 38, 56]. However, due to the limited
number of B. burgdorferi s.l. DNA isolates from questing ticks
analysed to genospecies level, we can not exclude the presence
of B. burgdorferi sensu stricto (s.s.), Borrelia lusitaniae, and/or
Borrelia spielmanii in our study sites, as their occurrence has
been reported from other locations of Slovakia [41, 57–59].
In contrast to the large amount of data on the ecology of
B
burgdorferi s.l., information on factors that determine the geo-
graphical spread and circulation of
B
. miyamotoi, its co-
circulation with Lyme disease spirochetes, and associations
to reservoir hosts, is still limited. In Europe, rodents
(Apodemus spp., M. glareolus) are suggested to be the main
reservoirs of B. miyamotoi, with infection prevalences up to
[19, 23, 31, 60, 61]. To our knowledge, the
prev-
alence of infection in the skin of A. flavicollis determined in
our study is so far the highest among the examined European
rodents. Our results further support findings on the importance
of M. glareolus [19, 23, 31] and A. flavicollis [23, 31] in the
maintenance of B. miyamotoi. Moreover, to the best of our
knowledge, our study provides the first evidence on the infec-
tion of wild-living rodents with B. miyamotoi from Slovakia
and co-infection of both I. ricinus ticks and rodents with
B
miyamotoi and B. burgdorferi s.l.

The associations of B. afzelii, B. burgdorferi s.s., and B.
bavariensis (with predominance of B. afzelii) with European
wild-living rodents has been proven by several studies and
extensively reviewed [38, 40, 41, 56, 62, 63]. Apodemus
spp. were found to be more heavily infested with I. ricinus
larvae than M. glareolus and M. arvalis, and the prevalence of
infection in mice was higher than in M. glareolus. However,
voles were more efficient than mice in transmitting B. afzelii
to feeding ticks [41, 64]. In contrast to previous findings, in
this study, the prevalence of infection with B. burgdorferi s.l.
was lower in A. flavicollis than M. glareolus. On the other
hand, the prevalence of
B
. miyamotoi was higher in mice than
voles. Interestingly, none of the examined M. arvalis skin was
infected with
B
. miyamotoi, although the prevalence of infec-
tion with B. burgdorferi s.l. was in this species the highest
among the tested rodents. B. miyamotoi-infected ticks and
rodents were found also at the location where M. arvalis were
captured. Because the number of examined M. arvalis speci-
mens was relatively low and only their skin was analysed, we
cannot draw final conclusions about the role of this rodent
species in the maintenance of
B
. miyamotoi. Nevertheless,
our findings raise questions about the susceptibility of differ-
ent rodent species to infection with
B
. miyamotoi and the
efficiency in transmitting spirochetes to ticks while pointing
to the necessity of further studies on the physiological mech-
anisms underlying rodent-tick-Borrelia interactions.
Based on the absence or extremely low rate of co-infected
ticks, it was previously thought that relapsing fever and Lyme
disease spirochetes do not share reservoir hosts [14]. This as-
sumption was also supported by the different modes of trans-
mission of the two groups of borreliae. While both horizontal
and transovarial transmission of B. miyamotoi exist in ticks [7,
27], the main route of infection of ticks with B. burgdorferi s.l.,
and particularly with B. afzelii, is by feeding on the blood of
infected hosts or co-feeding [63, 65]. However, the increasing
evidence of co-infections of B. burgdorferi s.l. and
B
miyamotoi in Ixodes spp. in Europe, Asia, and Northern
America indicate that these spirochetes may share amplifying
vertebrate hosts [9, 10, 12, 19, 54, 66]. In the present study,

sion cycles of the relapsing fever and Lyme disease spirochetes
may exist. Better understanding of the physiological and mo-
lecular processes underlying the survival, replication, and in-
teractions of the different spirochete species in ticks and rodents
is, however, needed.
We identified the same genotype of B. miyamotoi in
questing ticks and rodent skin. Sequence analysis revealed
high degree of identity with European isolates pathogenic to
humans that were detected in cerebrospinal fluid from a hu-
man patient (AB824730) and questing I. ricinus (AB824855)
in the Netherlands [35], or in questing (LC006118) and
rodent-attached I. ricinus from A. flavicollis (LC006120) in
Hungary [23]. Analysis of the B. burgdorferi s.l. IGS se-
quences revealed genetic variability of the B. afzelii and
B
garinii isolates and indicate that additional molecular analysis
considering other genomic regions is needed to determine the
pathogenicity of individual B. afzelii strains.
Furthermore, we identified
B
. miyamotoi and
B
burgdorferi s.l. in tick and rodent isolates throughout the study
(2011–2014) suggesting that the spirochetes are endemic in
the area and rodents are involved in their enzootic cycles.
Although no human cases of B. miyamotoi-associated relaps-
ing fever have been reported from Slovakia, our results indi-
cate that they may occur and co-transmission of the pathogen-
ic agents to humans may be possible.
Conclusions
We documented the presence of the same genotype of
B
miyamotoi in host-seeking I. ricinus ticks and in two rodent
species, A. flavicollis and M. glareolus, in southwestern
Slovakia. The genotype of B. miyamotoi shows high degree of
identity to genotypes described from ticks and human patients in
Europe. Ticks and rodents were also infected with B. burgdorferi
s.l., with dominance of B. afzelii. Co-infections of
B
. miyamotoi
and B. afzelii were revealed in ticks and rodents, suggesting co-
circulation of the two pathogenic bacteria and sharing vectors
and reservoir hosts in natural foci of the investigated area. Our
findings indicate that humans in Slovakia may be at risk of in-
fection with tick-borne relapsing fever, and in some cases togeth-
er with Lyme borreliosis. Moreover, they point to the importance
of co-infections of ticks and reservoir hosts with different patho-
genic microorganisms and their implications to public health.
